title: Goguette Bread Opens Hidden Wine Bar in Santa Rosa
summary:
Bistroquette de Goguette is a tiny hideaway with about 20 seats, inspired by childhood memories, good bread and the pleasure of doing absolutely nothing.

The post Goguette Bread Opens Hidden Wine Bar in Santa Rosa appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Open the door to Bistroquette de Goguette, and you step through a magic portal into a neighborhood wine bar in Paris. Not just any wine bar, but the place where owner Najine Shariat spent countless unhurried evenings with her family, sometimes falling asleep on a bench with her three sisters while their parents sipped wine and nibbled on bread and cheese.

It wasn’t a restaurant or a bar, really, but a third space where families could linger over a simple meal without spending much money or watching the clock. It wasn’t about the wine or the food; it was about the moment.

“My parents used to sit in a corner and grab a glass of wine, and no one would bother them. They could sit for three hours,” said Shariat.

Something almost unheard of in the United States: Who has three hours to drink wine and eat bread?

That’s precisely why Shariat has brought this cherished childhood memory to life, right down to the black-and-white mosaic floor tiles, wrought-iron bistro tables, long banquettes and dim lighting. Even the wall color, a hard-to-pin-down shade somewhere between dark forest green and midnight blue, is the same. Or at least pretty close, she said.

Now Shariat hopes to give her Sonoma County neighbors a little of what she remembers: a place to gather over a glass of wine and a basket of bread with salted butter.

A place to slow down, put away the phones and stay awhile.

Part speakeasy, part wine bar

The small wine bar adjoining Goguette Bread in Santa Rosa has no sign, no sandwich board with daily specials outside and no obvious indication that it’s even there. It’s intentionally hidden in plain sight, known mostly to Goguette regulars and through word of mouth. Reservations are recommended, though customers can check in at the bakery to see if there’s space.

“If you know, you know,” she said with a grin.

The secrecy isn’t about exclusion, but about keeping the space intimate, without pressure to turn tables quickly.

Shariat, who co-owns the Parisian bakery with her husband, Nas Salamati, said the adjoining space was originally intended for a larger production kitchen. At least, that’s what Salamati wanted. She had something very different in mind.

“I really wanted this for me,” she admitted. Salamati acquiesced.

The usually bubbly Shariat, dressed in a black-and-white striped shirt and white baker’s cap, pauses when the conversation turns to her mother, who died in May. Her eyes well up as she explains why opening the wine bar suddenly became so important.

“I had to do something,” she said of her decision in August to create Bistroquette.

What began as an idea for a neighborhood gathering spot, and a way to add seating to the busy bakery, became a tribute to her parents and the evenings they spent together in Paris.

Pointing around the room, she tells the story of each piece of furniture and art: mismatched antique mirrors from Southern California that she strapped to the roof of her car, impossibly heavy bistro tables from France, upholstered wooden church pews donated and installed by members of a Portuguese church, and her sister’s original artwork on the walls.

Bistroquette de Goguette is truly a labor of love. Emphasis on the labor. But also the love.

The menu

This is Goguette, of course, so bread always has a starring role.

The short Bistroquette menu includes a basket of assorted breads with French salted butter, charcuterie, baguette sandwiches — ham and cheese or ham and butter — and a green olive and roasted sweet pepper fougasse made especially for the wine bar.

“The idea is to keep it simple, not overwhelm people,” she said.

There’s also the bakery’s luscious custard-style ice cream — the chocolate-orange is outstanding — available by the cup or as an affogato with espresso. Apple juice is available for children, who are welcome at the wine bar.

Bistroquette’s wine list is equally straightforward, with six or seven French and Sonoma County wines chosen for their easy drinkability, mostly $10 to $14 a glass. The selection includes Champagne and other sparkling wines, fruity red Gamay served chilled, rosé and a couple of whites, usually a Chardonnay from Burgundy and a local Sauvignon Blanc.

Orders are placed through a small window looking into the bakery, keeping the setup casual. Shariat and Salamati stop by to visit with customers and friends but spend most of their time in the bakery, leaving guests to enjoy themselves at their own pace.

“This is just a place to be and in the moment, to be transported somewhere else,” Shariat said, “and then walk out and go on with your life.”

Bistroquette de Goguette: Adjoining Goguette Bread, 59 Montgomery Drive, Santa Rosa, goguettebread.com. Open 1:30-9 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday. Closed Sunday through Tuesday. Enter through the bakery and ask about seating. Reservations recommended by emailing info@goguettebread.com.

title: Sonoma Botanical Garden Offers Unique Autumn Leaf-Peeping Experience
summary:
Boasting over 50 species of wild-origin Asian maples, this public botanical garden in Glen Ellen is an ideal spot for viewing autumn-leaf hues.

The post Sonoma Botanical Garden Offers Unique Autumn Leaf-Peeping Experience appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The maple collection at Sonoma Botanical Garden in Glen Ellen offers visitors a unique and rare glimpse of autumn hues, making it an ideal spot for leaf-peeping on a sunny, crisp fall day.

The garden, founded almost 40 years ago, boasts more than 50 species of wild-origin Asian maples. As autumn’s shorter days and cooler nights unlock the maples’ gold, crimson, and even purple hues, November is an ideal time to engage in the Japanese tradition of momijigari — or autumn-leaf hunting.

The garden has several guided events through November, including a Fall Color Walk Nov. 13-22, but the park is open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily so visitors can explore the spectacle at their own pace.

The five-lobed maple (Acer pentaphyllum) is one of the last species to flaunt its crimson foliage, often extending the season into early December. While traveling to and from the garden along Highway 12, Sonoma Valley vineyards put on their own vibrant display, ensuring a flamboyant and fabulous fall outing.

12841 Highway 12, Glen Ellen. 707-996-3166, sonomabg.org

title: Mozaik Restaurant in Sonoma Gets Surprise Visit From Tyra Banks
summary:
“America’s Next Top Model” creator Tyra Banks surprised a local restaurant on the Sonoma Plaza with a recent visit.

The post Mozaik Restaurant in Sonoma Gets Surprise Visit From Tyra Banks appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Supermodel, actress and producer Tyra Banks traded the catwalk for a Sonoma stroll this week when she made a surprise visit to a Sonoma Plaza restaurant. The “America’s Next Top Model” creator and judge dined at Mozaik, the global cuisine-focused restaurant that replaced Sonoma’s Sausage Emporium in 2024.

Mozaik owner Miranda Ives, who founded Sausage Emporium in 2021 before expanding to gyros, poke bowls, umami burgers and Kashmiri tacos, took a selfie with Banks and posted it on Instagram after her visit.

“It was a lovely surprise in the middle of an already buzzing Friday evening,” the social media post stated regarding Banks’ visit.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by MOZAIK (@mozaik_sonoma)

The post also said Banks ordered the restaurant’s signature mashed potatoes and sticky ribs, while the rest of her party enjoyed Kashmiri tacos, Sichuan wontons and Thai green curry chicken.

Mozaik draws on Ives’ world travels, serving a diverse menu in a prime Plaza location. Last year, the restaurant added more outdoor seating and an accessible ramp.

In addition to “America’s Next Top Model,” Banks is known for her stint as a Victoria’s Secret Angel, hosting her own talk show, “The Tyra Banks Show,” and co-staring in Disney’s 2000 fantasy comedy “Life-Size” alongside Lindsay Lohan. Her talk show won a Daytime Emmy Award in 2008 and 2009. Banks was also the first Black woman featured on the covers of GQ magazine and the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue.

This wasn’t Banks’ first foray into Wine Country — in 2016, Banks and her mother went through an “intensive boot camp” experience at the Culinary Institute of America in Napa.

Banks’ visit to Mozaik is one of many celebrity sightings in Sonoma County, where the stars come to dine on world-class cuisine and even launch their own wine brands.

“Thank you, Tyra, for choosing Mozaik,” the restaurant’s Instagram post stated. “It was an absolute pleasure having you with us!”

Mozaik is located at 31 E. Napa St., Sonoma. 707-934-8814, mozaiksonoma.com

title: Alter Egos: Traditional Local Wine Brands Show Their Adventurous Side
summary:
Local winemakers are taking a chance on experimenting with wine. Here are three “dual-personality” brands in Wine Country worth discovering.

The post Alter Egos: Traditional Local Wine Brands Show Their Adventurous Side appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Newer wineries with a natural bent aren’t the only ones fermenting outside the box. Long-established producers are also branching out, and some have even launched adventurous side brands. The idea is to give winemakers a chance to have fun and experiment while offering consumers — especially younger ones — a variety of wine styles to explore.

Here are three “dual-personality” wineries worth discovering.

Kokomo Winery/Breaking Bread

Winemaker Erik Miller founded his Healdsburg winery in 2004 and built a reputation for producing terrific Dry Creek Zinfandel, Alexander Valley Cabernet Sauvignon and a delicious rosé. Then, in 2018, he introduced Breaking Bread. Made in a lighter, lower-alcohol style than the Kokomo offerings, the lineup includes Zinfandel-based pet-nat and rosé, along with an orange wine, a whole cluster Pinot Noir, and Al Dente, a chillable Mourvèdre blend. Taste them at the Kokomo tasting room in Healdsburg. 4791 Dry Creek Road, Healdsburg, kokomowines.com; breakingbreadwines.com

Stewart Cellars/Guthrie Family Wines

When he’s not making serious, terroir-driven wines for Yountville-based Stewart Cellars — founded in 2000 by his father-in-law Michael Stewart — Blair Guthrie makes his own brand of wines at Guthrie Family Cellars in Sonoma. Guthrie takes a minimalist approach, starting with organically and biodynamically farmed grapes. Flavor profiles are bright and fresh, shining a spotlight on varieties such as Vermentino, Grenache Blanc and Gamay Noir. 6752 Washington St., Yountville, stewartcellars.com; guthriefamilywines.com

Obsidian Ridge/Rabbit Hole

Brothers Arpad and Peter Molnar launched Obsidian Ridge, their Lake County-based Cabernet Sauvignon brand, in 2002. Then, in 2020, they went down a rabbit hole. The Rabbit Hole line is a little on the wild side, taking an experimental, natural-leaning path. Current releases include a sparkling Pinot Noir pet-nat called Pezsgő, the Máslás red piquette and a sweet white vermouth. Taste the wines at Obsidian Ridge Base Camp in downtown Sonoma. 441 First St. W., Sonoma, obsidianwineco.com

This story was excerpted from our feature on Sonoma County Wineries Building a Brighter Future, originally published in the September/October 2026 issue of Sonoma Magazine.

title: Where to Get the Best Nachos in Sonoma County
summary:
Nov. 6 is National Nacho Day. Here's where to find the best of the cheesy dish in Sonoma County.

The post Where to Get the Best Nachos in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The perfect dish for sharing, the ultimate Super Bowl snack, the pub favorite you can’t resist — nachos are the quintessential cheesy treat.

We have Ignacio “Nacho” Anaya García to thank for this simple yet glorious dish.

According to the commonly told origin story, in 1943, a group of U.S. military wives arrived at Club Victoria in Piedras Negras, Mexico, where García worked. With no chefs available to prepare a meal, he improvised: he topped tortilla chips with grated cheese, broiled them until melted and finished the dish with sliced jalapeños.

He called his creation “Nachos especiales,” or Nacho’s special. The world has been indebted to his genius ever since.

There’s no wrong time to enjoy a plate, but National Nacho Day, Nov. 6, offers a particularly good excuse. From traditional Mexican-style nachos to creative takes piled high with barbecue, here are some Sonoma County spots worth visiting.

Sonoma

El Dorado Cantina

Also known as EDK Cantina, this takeout-only spot at the Eldorado Hotel serves nachos with black beans, Chihuahua cheese, pickled carrots, jalapeños, pico de gallo and crema. Add chicken, al pastor, carnitas or short rib birria. 405 First St. W., Sonoma, 707-996-3030, eldoradosonoma.com/edk-cantina

Juanita Juanita

This hidden gem outside downtown Sonoma is a locals’ favorite. Nachos come in meaty or meatless versions, with chips, beans, cheese, guacamole, cotija cheese, jalapeños, salsa and sour cream. 19114 Arnold Drive, Sonoma, 707-935-3981, juanitajuanita.com, instagram.com/juanitajuanita2

Sonoma Eats

Reopened this year in the former La Hacienda space, Sonoma Eats serves loaded nachos topped with beans, cheese, onion, salsa, crema, guacamole and cilantro. Add chorizo, chicken, carne asada, birria or mushrooms. 561 Fifth St. W., Sonoma, 707-996-1783, instagram.com/meetme_sonomaeats

Petaluma

Lagunitas Brewing Company

A natural pairing for an IPA, the Brewhouse Nachos feature housemade IPA beer cheese, black beans, pickled jalapeños, olives, salsa and sour cream. 1280 N. McDowell Blvd., Petaluma, 707-778-8776, lagunitas.com/en-us/taproom

Rohnert Park

Don Julio’s Rincon Latin Grill & Pupusas

Although pupusas are a specialty, the restaurant’s Locos Nachos are just as delicious. Crispy corn tortilla chips are topped with refried beans, cheese, guacamole, sour cream, pico de gallo and a choice of tender marinated meat. A vegetarian version is also available. 217 Southwest Blvd., Rohnert Park, 707-242-3160, donjulioslatingrill.com

El Rancho Taqueria

A popular stop for students from nearby Rancho Cotate High School and Sonoma State University, this unassuming strip-mall restaurant serves crispy super nachos piled with melted cheese, beans, guacamole, pico de gallo, sour cream and choice of meat. A vegetarian version is also available. 1451 Southwest Blvd., Rohnert Park, 707-795-8537

Santa Rosa

El Roy’s Mexican Grill

Nacho connoisseurs flock to El Roy’s for generously portioned super nachos layered with melted cheese, refried beans, tender meat, fresh pico de gallo, jalapeños, sour cream and guacamole. Available only at the Santa Rosa restaurant and drive-thru. 602 Elsa Drive, Santa Rosa; elroys.com

Gio y Los Magos

This Roseland food truck serves Magic Nachos perfect for sharing — birria tortilla chips piled high with cheese, guacamole, sour cream, carnitas, diced onions, jalapeños and cilantro. 100 Sebastopol Road, Santa Rosa, instagram.com/gioylosmagos

La Rosa Tequileria

A downtown destination for margaritas and Mexican comfort food, La Rosa serves nachos layered with melted cheeses, crema, guacamole, refried beans, salsa and jalapeños atop crisp corn tortilla chips. Add carnitas, pollo asado, carne asada and beef birria. 500 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-523-3663, larosasantarosa.com

Los Arcos

These super nachos are a meat lover’s dream. Tortilla chips are buried under a mountain of meat (carne asada is recommended), along with beans, cheese, pico de gallo, guacamole and a dollop of sour cream. You may need utensils for this one. 1791 Marlow Road, Suite 6, Santa Rosa, 707-545-5858, losarcosrestaurantsr.com

Parkside Eats

The sister restaurant to Sonoma Eats opened in April with a menu of American and Mexican comfort food. Its ahi tuna poke nachos are a chef favorite, with quality tuna, pickled onions, cucumber and avocado atop wonton chips, finished with Sriracha aioli. 4323 Montgomery Drive, Santa Rosa, 707-800-7466, parkside-eats.com

Taqueria Molcajetes

Known locally and nationally famous for its food and appearance on Guy Fieri’s “Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives,” Taqueria Molcajetes serves heaping plates of super nachos topped with cheese, beans, jalapeños, guacamole, sour cream and a choice of meat. 1195 W. College Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-544-8280

Sebastopol

Salt & Sea

Opened last year by Sushi Kosho chef Jake Rand at The Barlow, this fast-casual restaurant specializes in poke bowls, Japanese sandwiches and acai bowls. Its spicy tuna nachos feature fresh ahi tuna, tobiko, pineapple, crema and avocado atop fried wontons. 6760 McKinley St., Suite 130, Sebastopol, saltandseapoke.com

The Wild Poppy

This Sebastopol cafe and market has two locations, including one at The Barlow. Both serve “Cosmic Nachos,” made with fresh corn tortilla chips, black bean puree, “cosmic” queso, cashew crema, coleslaw, scallion and pepita chimichurri. The dish is vegan, but diners can add a poached egg or grilled chicken. 6780 McKinley St., Suite 160, and 9890 Bodega Highway, Sebastopol; 707-503-6332, thewildpoppycafe.com

Viva Mexicana

Vegans and vegetarians have plenty of options at Viva Mexicana. The vegan nachos are made with Daiya vegan cheese, refried beans, jalapeños, guacamole and pico de gallo. The vegetarian version of the Super Duper Nachos come topped with housemade potato and yam hash browns. 841 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol, 707-823-5555, vivamexicana.com

West County and Sonoma Coast

Guerneville Taco Truck

The family-owned local favorite offers consistently satisfying Mexican food and a reliably loaded plate of Nachos Supreme for your noshing pleasure. 16405 Highway 116, Guerneville, guernevilletacotruck.com

Ginochio’s Kitchen

Alicia’s Crackling Nachos combine barbecue and Mexican flavors, with a choice of pulled pork, tri-tip or beef brisket, plus melted cheese, mild chipotle sauce, avocado and sour cream. 1410 Bay Flat Road, Bodega Bay, 707-377-4359, ginochioskitchen.com

Multiple locations

El Gallo Negro

Known for its Oaxacan cuisine, El Gallo Negro serves nachos on a bed of housemade corn tortilla chips with beans, jack cheese, guacamole and sour cream. 8465 Old Redwood Highway, Windsor; 128 Plaza St., Healdsburg; 707-838-9511, elgallonegro.net

Fogbelt Brewing Company

Both locations feature elote nachos on the pub menu. Housemade tortilla chips are topped with chorizo, sweet corn, green onions, cotija cheese, cilantro, lime crema and jalapeño queso sauce. 1305 Cleveland Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-978-3400; 410 Hudson St., Healdsburg, 707-473-8532; fogbeltbrewing.com

Los Molcajetes Bar & Grill

The birria nachos are loaded with jack cheese, guacamole, salsa verde, grilled corn, black beans, pico de gallo, chipotle aioli, sour cream and cilantro. 1950 Piner Road, Suite 130, Santa Rosa, 707-843-4716; 6599 Montecito Blvd., Suite 110, Santa Rosa, 707-791-7571; 19101 Sonoma Highway, Sonoma, 707-935-3287; losmolcajetesbarandgrill.com

The post Where to Get the Best Nachos in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.

title: Historic Sonoma Barn With Modern Amenities Hits the Market
summary:
The Sonoma estate, salvaged from an 1840s New Jersey barn, retains its antique charm while providing modern touches.

The post Historic Sonoma Barn With Modern Amenities Hits the Market appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A barn-turned-residence on 2.8 acres in Sonoma is currently listed for sale. With three bedrooms, three bathrooms and a combined 4,450 square feet of living space, the main home and detached guesthouse are priced at $4,950,000.

The historic barn — located on an open meadow with views of Sonoma Mountain — had a previous life in Neshanic, New Jersey. In 2007, designer Barbara Johnsen arranged for a circa-1840 barn to be salvaged and moved across the country. 

Johnsen tapped Santa Rosa architect Sara Woodfield to convert the antique structure into a home. The silo, added to enclose a circular staircase, provides an on-theme focal point. A weathervane-topped cupola skylight illuminates the great room while adding to the barn’s unique, cinematic presence.

The structure maintains its original rough-hewn and weight-bearing barn frame. Exposed-wood trusses crown the space with historic charm while the white walls and numerous French doors create an airiness.

The home has been updated with modern amenities including high-speed internet, integrated AV, Sonos audio and solar. Current homeowners collaborated with furniture maker Josh Podoll and interior architect Karyn Gabriel to transform the interiors.

Finishes are modern and luxe, from dramatically proportioned marble pieces to walnut floors. Contemporary light fixtures, rich-toned millwork and select deep-toned walls add drama and a pleasing transitional quality to the scheme.

Some of the barn’s original floors were installed by the property’s current listing agent, Matt Sevenau, who owned a flooring showroom in Sonoma before parlaying his home knowledge into a real estate career. Sevenau appreciates the “full-circle” experience of listing the property he witnessed transform 20 years ago.

The grounds include a seasonal creek, olive and fruit trees, raised beds, a bocce court and a sunset porch. The pool receives early evening sunlight.

Sevenau said for the right person, the barn would be like winning the lottery, as there are no other properties like it in Sonoma.

For more information on this property at 21831 Schellville Road in Sonoma, contact listing agents Matt Sevenau, 707-934-5630, Compass, 591 Broadway, Sonoma; or Erin Lial, 707-333-5596, Coldwell Banker, 1200 Main St., St. Helena. dospalmassonoma.com

title: These Sonoma County Wineries Are Farming for the Future
summary:
As new Sonoma County wineries make strides toward sustainability, they join others who have pushed the region forward for decades.

The post These Sonoma County Wineries Are Farming for the Future appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Vance Rose reaches out and plucks a few leaves off a tall, twisting bay laurel tree. I lift them to my nose and smell the powerful, herbaceous aroma. “I love bay laurel,” he says. “It is so lovely.”

A bay laurel tree might not seem to have much to do with wine, but as we hop in a golf cart and drive around Harper’s Rest, a new winery in Russian River Valley named for Reuben Harper, the farmer who originally tended this land in the 19th century, it quickly becomes clear that Rose sees the property not just as a vineyard, but as a holistic, living organism.

He points out the cover crops growing from the untilled soil between the vine rows, the beehives next to the pond, the chicken coop laden with fresh eggs, the garden where he grows produce for the culinary program, the lichen-coated boulders around the tasting room.

Harper’s Rest debuted last year after Young’s Holdings CEO Chris Underwood bought the Healdsburg estate (formerly Arista Winery) and is establishing itself as a standard bearer for sustainability. Rose is not only its winemaker, but its chief apostle for regenerative farming. As we sip Pinot Noir and Chardonnay at an oak-shaded table outside the tasting room, he explains why.

“Organic is pretty straightforward,” he says. “You can’t kill bugs, you can’t kill weeds, and you can’t kill mold with a synthetic, but you can do any of those three things with organic material. Regenerative, you have to be certified organic, but you cannot use even organic herbicide. You can’t kill any weeds, and you can’t till.” One reason, Rose explains, is that microbes aerate soil and provide nutrition to vines. Sprays — even organic ones — and tilling kill those microbes.

The vineyards on the estate around us are still in the certification process, but the winery’s Moon Dust Vineyard, on a plot outside Sebastopol, is already Regenerative Organic Certified (ROC). Rose tells an anecdote from the brutal heat wave during the 2022 harvest, when temperatures soared to 113 degrees, that provides evidence of the impact: “We have a neighbor who grows grapes, he tills, and we took our soil temperature, and we took his less than 20 yards away. Our soil, with this permanent cover crop, was 34 degrees colder than his.” Rose says elevated soil temperatures can stop ripening and cause vine roots to strangle. “We came through 113.2 degrees, not a problem in the world,” he concludes. “He had serious issues.”

Conscientious farming is just one way in which Sonoma County vintners are pushing the envelope when it comes to sustainability. Later that afternoon, I’m on the terrace at Skipstone, another winery that looks out across a California Certified Organic Farmers (CCOF)-certified vineyard in Alexander Valley. General manager Patricia Smith and I turn our gaze from the terraced vines to the winery’s new stone building, which she believes is on its way to being certified LEED Platinum, the highest rating granted by the U.S. Green Building Council, an accomplishment only one other winery in the county — Silver Oak, also in Alexander Valley — has managed. Skipstone’s facility is cut deep into the hillside, reducing the energy needed to cool the solar-powered building, and is constructed of reclaimed redwood and stone quarried on the property.

“One of the things [USGBC assessors] really want to make sure of is building materials and where they’re coming from,” Smith explains. “So, using materials that we’re not flying over from France or Italy, but having stuff that, literally, we dug it up over there, we cracked it, and then we placed it here.” She points to a dark patch in the facade, indicative of volcanic rock, and adds, “It’s also kind of cool, you can see our terroir in the wall.”

While Harper’s Rest and Skipstone may be new leaders in sustainability, there are many local pioneers who have spent decades blazing that trail. Duff Bevill of Bevill Vineyard Management, who began his career in Dry Creek Valley in 1973, remembers working under Joe Vogensen, who was already practicing no-till farming.

“He was the only guy in the valley to do it,” Bevill says. “And when I went on my own, I incorporated something similar. It was hard for me to convince my clients. The first one was Dave Stare at Dry Creek Vineyard, and he thought we were doing something wrong. I said, ‘No, it’s good for the soil.’”

In those days, the concept of organic farming existed, but Bevill says that the main focus was pesticides. Like Rose, he points out that “you still use pesticides. Back then, the emphasis was primarily on whether it was chemical-free or chemical-reduced.”

By the year 2000, sustainability had become a buzzword, and the Sonoma County Grape Growers Association (now Sonoma County Winegrowers, or SCW) began a framework for its members. The initial program was a self-assessment that had been developed by the Lodi-Woodbridge Winegrape Commission, and which vintners could use to judge themselves environmentally, socially, and economically. “You could get into becoming an organic farm model within the sustainability system, but it had so many other categories that were valuable to assess as a grower,” Bevill says. “Are we polluting the air? Are we good to our employees? Are we good to our community? That’s all part of that program.”

The nature of a self-assessed program led to accusations of greenwashing, so the SCW later moved toward using third-party evaluators. According to SCW CEO Karissa Kruse, a qualifying certification can come from the California Sustainable Winegrowing Alliance, the Lodi Rules, Sustainability in Practice (SIP), or Fish Friendly Farming. In 2014, the organization made a commitment to have 100% of its vineyards certified sustainable within five years. Today, the number stands at 99%.

A common critique is that the stringency of the requirements varies based on the organization. “I work with all sorts of different people,” Rose says. “They all say, ‘Oh yeah, I’m on the Sonoma County sustainable thing.’ I’m like, ‘You’re spraying chemicals. That is not sustainable.’ That standard is way too low.” So, many wineries seek to go further, getting certified organic by CCOF, regenerative by the Regenerative Organic Alliance (ROA), or biodynamic by the Demeter Association.

Biodynamics, conceived by Austrian philosopher Rudolf Steiner in the 1920s, shares many tenets with the regenerative framework, looking at a farm as a fully integrated organism that includes soil, plants, and animals. It also incorporates some mystical elements — emphasizing phases of the moon and burying cow horns stuffed with humus and manure. Benziger Family Winery on Sonoma Mountain began converting to biodynamic farming in 1993 and was the first winery in the county to earn a Demeter certification in 2000. Vintner Chris Benziger says he doesn’t necessarily buy into the spiritual aspects of the system, but he’s a true believer in the practical impacts.

“I grew up in the city, and coming out here, there’s all these critters I’ve never seen before — wild turkeys, jackrabbits, bobcats, foxes,” Benziger recalls of the early years on his property in the ’80s and early ’90s when his family was still using commercial pest and weed management chemicals. “Once we would spray, you wouldn’t see any of those critters. By the fourth year, it was silent. And I noticed that the soil was almost changing colors. This soil that had been knitted together with billions of microorganisms was being killed. Here we were professing that we found this gorgeous piece of property that we absolutely loved, yet we were farming it in a way that felt irresponsible.” Today, Benziger not only farms biodynamically, but also offers tractor tours on which interested guests can learn about it.

Visitors to Littorai, outside Sebastopol, also get a lesson in biodynamics during estate tours past compost piles and a shed where the crew prepares teas using native plants to enrich the soil. Littorai winemaker Ted Lemon spent his early career in France. “The 1980s in Burgundy was really the height of conventional farming,” he says. “That’s what I was kind of raised in. I just got to the point where I felt like I was the hamster in its cage going around and around on its exercise wheel. You could go faster and faster, and Western agronomy would ask for more and more inputs.” He studied a variety of agroecological approaches, and he and his wife, Heidi, settled on biodynamics when they bought the Littorai estate in 2000.

Unlike Benziger, Lemon gets into the metaphysical side of the system. “It’s a form of spiritual agriculture,” he says. “It’s the belief that the spiritual world exists, and it manifests itself in all things around us.” He acknowledges that it sounds a bit woo-woo, and admits he was skeptical at first, but the effects of biodynamics — not tilling, promoting cover crop diversity — were undeniable. “I remember in 2009, a year where the first rain of any significance was enormous,” he says, “and I walked out to the bottom of the Pivot Vineyard, and there was no erosion. There were no little rivulets of dirt or anything. It’s like, ‘Oh my goodness, this is really working.’” As for the wine, he adds, “When you look at the measures of a juice panel of grapes, of the nutrient status for the yeast, they’re highest in the biodynamic vineyards.”

While Lemon’s estate would qualify for just about any sustainability certification, he hasn’t pursued any of them. “Anybody who wants to criticize us for that, I totally accept the criticism,” he says. “And people who do the work to get a certification deserve their certification. All I care about is the work on the ground.”

A big hurdle for sustainable farming, given the wine industry’s current downturn, is the expense. Lemon estimates he spends about $1,000 more per acre; Benziger ballparks his costs at around 10% higher. Rose recalls it costing about 6% more per ton to farm organically, and more still for regenerative, in part because labor costs are higher (both because there’s more manual labor involved and because the ROA requires better pay for workers). But cost to him is irrelevant. “I would be organic if it were 50% more expensive,” he says, “because I don’t want to drink that shit.”

Benziger points out that the gap shrinks over time. “They always talk about the initial farming costs, and they are more expensive, but you get better quality wine, and hopefully you can charge more,” he says. He also points out that the typical lifespan of a grapevine is 20 to 25 years, whereas his are 35 to 40 years old. “We’re getting an extra lifespan. And after planting a vineyard, what’s the most expensive thing you can do? Replant. That’s $40,000, probably more now, an acre.”

Even taking the long view, the economic situation for many farmers is bleak. “Agriculture is hurting more than it’s hurt since the Great Depression,” says Carlo Mondavi, who makes Sonoma Coast wines at RAEN Winery. “I’m not just talking about viticulture; I’m talking about corn and soy and veggies, all of it. It’s very difficult to be preachy and tell someone not to do something when they can barely put food on their family’s table.”

Still, this perspective hasn’t stopped Mondavi, the grandson of Napa legend Robert Mondavi, from believing sustainability is paramount. He saw firsthand the impact of chemical inputs when he was just 24, after his family sold Robert Mondavi Winery in 2004.

“We lived on a ranch, and there was a vineyard that separated my grandfather and my father’s house,” he says. The first year after the sale to Constellation Brands, he noticed the grass beneath the vines was turning yellow and orange. “I pulled [my father] outside, and he said, ‘Oh, they’re chemically mowing.’ And I was like, ‘Why would you spray a chemical by the root ball of a plant that you’re trying to grow? Wouldn’t it hurt the plant?’ And the dirt I was standing on was directly above the well where my father and my grandfather split the drinking water, and I said, ‘Wouldn’t we end up drinking this?’”

Mondavi later discovered that coastal California’s monarch butterfly population had decreased by more than 95% since the commercial introduction of Roundup, so in 2016, he issued the Monarch Challenge, calling for farmers to stop using these chemicals. He also became the chief farming officer at Monarch Tractor, which produced autonomous, electric tractors to help cut emissions.

Despite a promising start, Monarch Tractor ceased operations at the beginning of this year, but that setback doesn’t indicate a dead end. Sonoma County Winegrowers has partnered with companies such as John Deere on a “Farm of the Future” project to explore technological advancements. “I think, as we go forward, we’re going to start to be looked at as not only a sustainability leader, but an innovation leader,” says Tyler Klick, co-owner of Redwood Empire Vineyard Management and chair of the SCW board of directors.

Mondavi sounds a similarly optimistic note. “The technology’s arriving at the same time as consumer knowledge and desire are meeting,” he says. “I think that Sonoma will be one of the first fully organic wine regions in the world. When you look more particularly on the West Sonoma Coast, we’re already basically there. [We’re] far ahead of almost any other region in the United States that I know of, which is pretty exciting.”

title: Graton’s Underwood Bar & Bistro Sold After 24 Years to Owners of Lo & Behold
summary:
The owners of a popular Healdsburg cocktail bar and restaurant will take the reins of the west county institution. But don't expect anything to radically change.

The post Graton’s Underwood Bar & Bistro Sold After 24 Years to Owners of Lo & Behold appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
After nearly 24 years of steak frites, chou-fleur and Hemingways, Graton’s Underwood Bar & Bistro is changing hands. The good news for its loyal customers: Three of the restaurant’s biggest fans are taking over.

Matthew Greenbaum, who opened the beloved west county restaurant in December 2002, has sold Underwood to Sean Kelley, Tara Heffernon and Laura Sanfilippo, the trio behind Healdsburg’s popular Lo & Behold Bar + Kitchen.

Kelley started as a line cook at Underwood in 2004 and worked his way up to sous chef and co-manager over 12 years. He’s stayed close to Greenbaum ever since and isn’t about to fix what isn’t broken.

“This place is a legacy restaurant with a loyal following. We just want to breathe a little new life into it,” Kelley said.

He knows every nook and cranny of the restaurant, and Greenbaum had joked for years that Kelley should buy it someday. Now, he’s finally taking him up on the offer. Greenbaum’s last official day will be New Year’s Eve.

“I’ve been thinking about it for some time. I’m ready to free up some of my time, and my brain space, to move on to my third act,” said Greenbaum, 65.

That means more time for poetry, travel, creativity and his letterpress studio. But he’s quick to note he’s not heading for a rocking chair anytime soon.

Greenbaum will continue operating Willow Wood Market Cafe, the casual restaurant he opened across the street in 1995. Longtime Underwood general manager Jen Warfel will move there as well.

“Success for me is a new relationship with time,” he said.

That means fewer daily headaches from running a restaurant. And more time for whatever comes next.

A new era

When Greenbaum arrived in the sleepy, apple-processing town in the early 1990s, Graton had a couple of dive bars and plenty of empty buildings. Hitching posts for horses still lined the sidewalks.

Underwood, with its dark interior, red banquettes, nickel bar and Parisian bistro tiles, was an unlikely attraction in the tiny hamlet. It quickly became a gathering place for local winemakers, restaurant workers and neighbors drawn to Greenbaum’s classic French brasserie cooking and the cocktails.

Together, Willow Wood and Underwood helped turn quiet Graton into a dining destination.

“Everything about Underwood I built, designed, and it’s my baby,” he said. “The thought of selling it was hard.”

Finding the right people to take over made the decision easier.

“They understand Underwood well,” he said. “They don’t want to rewrite the script.”

Kelley, Heffernon and Sanfilippo opened Lo & Behold in 2022, building a loyal following for its inventive cocktails, globally inspired comfort food and lively, unpretentious atmosphere.

Heffernon and Sanfilippo were part of the founding team at Duke’s Spirited Cocktails, alongside Cappy Sorentino and Steven Maduro, in 2016. The bar became known for incorporating backyard botanicals into its drinks, helping fuel a craft cocktail movement that has since become commonplace.

The two left Duke’s in 2021 and later joined forces with Kelley, who had run the food program at Burdock, to open Lo & Behold.

“Underwood is a magical place to all three of us. We’re aware of how special a place it is to share a meal and memory,” Sanfilippo said.

The trio hopes to preserve what customers love about Underwood while adding a few touches of their own.

Kelley plans to lean into the restaurant’s original French brasserie roots, with a nod to classic San Francisco dishes such as cioppino. Steak frites and chou-fleur will stay, as will cocktails rooted in the classics.

The biggest changes will include online reservations, a reimagined happy hour and the return of lunch service. Heffernon and Sanfilippo will split their time between Healdsburg and Graton, while Kelley oversees the kitchen transition. Current chef Mark Miller will stay on.

For Greenbaum, the handoff is as much about the people as the place. Finding owners who would look after Underwood’s longtime employees and loyal customers was a priority. He’s confident he’s found them.

He also doesn’t plan to be a stranger.

“I feel like Underwood is going to stay and be there another 25 years,” Greenbaum said, “and I’ll be sitting there having a cocktail.”

title: Rhône-Style Wines and 360-Degree Views Set the Stage at Trattore Farms in Geyserville
summary:
From seasonal paninis and panoramic patio views to ATV tours and estate olive oil tastings, Trattore Farms offers an elevated Wine Country experience in Geyserville.

The post Rhône-Style Wines and 360-Degree Views Set the Stage at Trattore Farms in Geyserville appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Lots of Silicon Valley tech entrepreneurs get bitten by the wine bug. But in Tim Bucher’s case, it was the other way around. Bucher is a wine guy who got bitten by the tech bug.

Raised on his family’s Dry Creek Valley dairy farm, Bucher grew up around legendary winemaking families like the Gallos and Seghesios. While kids his age collected baseball cards, Bucher became fascinated with grapes and wine. At 16, he began growing wine grapes on a 2-acre property he bought with his siblings.

While studying agriculture at UC Davis, Bucher says he “accidentally” switched to computer and electrical engineering. He continued that path at Stanford University and later worked in the technology industry for firms such as Apple and Microsoft.

Despite Bucher’s success in the tech world, farming kept calling him back to Sonoma County. In 1998, he and his wife Mary Louise bought a 40-acre property in Dry Creek Valley and planted it with grapevines and olive trees.

After years of development, the couple launched Dry Creek Olive Co. in the early 2000s, producing estate olive oils and vinegars. They released their first Trattore Farms wines in 2004, naming the winery after the Italian word for tractor. They opened their hilltop winery facility in 2015.

Bucher’s agriculture and technology worlds eventually merged when he grew concerned about rising farm labor costs and regulations. To ease the pressure, Bucher created automated systems for Trattore Farms, including remote-controlled irrigation systems and an autonomous tractor equipped with electric motors, cameras and computers.

At the urging of his Silicon Valley friends, he turned those innovations into a company called Agtonomy. The AI and software services firm helps wineries and farms turn standard tractors and other industrial equipment into autonomous, remotely controlled machinery.

Today, Trattore Farms and Winery sustainably farms 22 varieties of wine grapes and 20 types of olives, using practices such as no-till farming, water recycling and soil-enhancing compost made from grape and olive pomace.

Focusing on Rhône varieties and Zinfandel, winemaker Craig Strehlow produces about 4,500 cases per year.

The vibe

Set amid steep slopes carpeted with vineyards and olive groves, Trattore’s Mediterranean-inspired hilltop winery near Geyserville is 400 feet above the valley floor. The tasting room doubles as a tractor showroom, with various models displayed among bottles of estate olive oils, vinegars and cute ceramic dishes.

As cool as the tractors are, the real show is out on the veranda. There, 360-degree views of Dry Creek Valley mesmerize tasters seated on the expansive patio. The tasting room also offers plenty of bar and table seating for rainy-day visits.

On the palate

Bubbles are always a great place to start, especially when the offering is as intriguing as the 2025 Bolle de Trattore ($58). Aromatic and peachy, with apple notes, the wine combines Picpoul and Viognier.

For a medium-bodied red with strawberry and tobacco spice aromas and ripe raspberry flavor, try the lively 2022 Dry Creek Valley Estate Grenache ($44). The 2022 Dry Creek Valley Proprietor’s Reserve GSM ($60) draws you in with perfumed aromas, then seals the deal with notes of red fruits and spice.

Wine tastings range from $30 for a discovery sampling to $45 for a flight paired with small bites. Olive oil and vinegar tastings cost $30 and include warm bread for dipping. Visitors can also order wines by the glass ($15-$20) and mocktails ($20 per flight or $10 per glass).

For the full experience, the Get Your Boots Dirty Tour ($125) includes an ATV excursion through the property’s rolling hills, stopping along the way to learn about Trattore’s vines and olive trees — one is nearly two centuries old and still producing fruit. You’ll also visit the olive mill to learn how a 4-ton stone mill transforms olives into luscious oils. The experience finishes with a tasting of wines, olive oils and vinegars.

Beyond the bottle

If you find yourself wanting to linger after your tasting, why not stay for lunch? Along with snacks such as seasoned nuts, Trattore Farms offers charcuterie boards, seasonal panini and entrée salads dressed with housemade olive oils and vinegars. You can also order “barcuterie” for your furry friend. Check the website for wood-fired pizza days.

Trattore Farms and Winery, 7878 Dry Creek Road, Geyserville. Open from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Thursday through Monday. 707-431-7200, trattorefarms.com

Tina Caputo is a wine, food, and travel writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including SevenFifty Daily, Visit California, HuffPost, and Sonoma magazine. Follow Tina on Instagram @winebroad and view her website at tinacaputo.com.

title: European-Style Villa in Santa Rosa Hits the Market
summary:
The Sonoma Mountain home in Santa Rosa features unique architectural details from around the world along with a pool, spa and guest cottage.

The post European-Style Villa in Santa Rosa Hits the Market appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A European-style home on 11.65 acres on Sonoma Mountain is currently listed for sale. The three-bedroom, three-bathroom home with a cottage, gardens and pool is priced at $3,775,000.

The main home, built in 2006, is traditionally styled with a stucco exterior, a rounded tower, turning stairways and a clay tile roof. Grapevines climb the dwelling in classic Mediterranean fashion.  

The interior is punctuated with unique architectural details and finishes, many of which are sourced from around the world. Traditional elements include ochre plaster walls, high ceilings and exposed wood beams. Colorful tile, Rondel windows, turned columns and repurposed oversized doors enliven the space. Showstopping arched windows and balconies with intricate ironwork yield to the stunning valley views.

The great room is grandly designed with columns, arches and a Rumford fireplace. The kitchen area has Caesarstone countertops, rustic cabinetry and a reclaimed door in a distressed blue. 

The grounds include stone terraces and stone paths that lead to gardens with flowering arbors and fruit trees. Covered decks include automatic screens and spots for lounging and dining. The pool, spa, dining areas and guesthouse enjoy panoramic views of the Mayacamas mountains.

For more information on this property at 6640 Sonoma Mountain Road in Santa Rosa, contact listing agents Tina Shone, 707-799-7556, or Evan Shone, 707-328-9288, 707-933-1515; Sotheby’s International Realty – Wine Country – Sonoma Brokerage, 793 Broadway, Sonoma. sothebysrealty.com/eng/sales/detail/180-l-1188-gt768e/6640-sonoma-mountain-road-santa-rosa-ca-95404
